newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's Grace-Hollogne, town of two scandals.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's Grace-Hollogne, town of two scandals.

text.p: One month ago, even most Belgians had never heard of this little town in the rolling hills outside Liege, where overgrown slagheaps bear witness to a great industrial past.
Now the name of Grace-Hollogne has travelled far beyond the country's borders, and for the worst possible reasons.

In June 1995, eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo disappeared while on a short walk near their homes. Four weeks ago, police dug up their bodies in the garden of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux in nearby Charleroi.
The masses of flowers at the Russo and Lejeune houses had not even wilted when Grace-Hollogne was thrust into the spotlight again.
On September 8, former mayor Alain Van der Biest was arrested and charged with the murder of fellow socialist politician Andre Cools in 1991.

Along with Van der Biest, who had been mayor for nearly 20 years, police arrested his former personal secretary Richard Taxquet, once a Grace-Hollogne policeman, and four members of the sizeable local Italo-Belgian community here.

"This town is not damned, but I am ashamed that the six people arrested in the Cools case have all lived here at some point," Maurice Mottard, who succeeded Van der Biest as mayor in January, told Reuters.
Grace-Hollogne may not be damned, but it is not a happy place. At the start of the century the town had the biggest zinc factory in Europe, countless coal mines and a booming steel industry.
Like much of the rest of Wallonia -- the southern, French-speaking half of Belgium -- Grace-Hollogne is now an industrial rustbelt with record unemployment of 25 percent.
Equally typical for Wallonia, the town is in the unshakeable grip of the Socialist Party (PS), which has governed without interruption since 1908.

Like the Christian-Democratic party (CVP) in the northern, Dutch-speaking half of Belgium, the PS permeates every layer of government, names judges and policemen and places its supporters at the head of state-owned industries.

In this web of political, social and financial power, Cools was the absolute kingmaker. The main question facing investigators is whether his murder was the result of the system that he had helped create.
Grace-Hollogne residents have little doubt about that.

"The Dutroux affair could have happened anywhere. But the Cools murder, that is the result of the all the sleazy scheming that went on here," said a Grace-Hollogne policeman, a one-time collegue of Taxquet.
Most Grace-Hollogne residents agree that their former mayor was not the kind of man to commission a murder.

"Van der Biest liked a drink, yes. But he does not have the guts to order Cools's murder, he is too weak for that," said a Grace-Hollogne pensioner who often met Van der Biest in the cafes close to his modest terraced house in rue Jean Jaures.
Residents described Van der Biest, who is the author of four novels, as an intellectual.
"He was a poet lost in the world of politics. The man I have known was incapable of masterminding a murder," Mayor Mottard said.
